scenes.title: Start with the claim
scenes.narration: Choose a format after stating the claim. A concept explanation can check understanding. A recent-context conversation explores relevance. A task walkthrough can observe a bounded action. No single format proves every part of a venture.

scenes.title: Compare small options
scenes.narration: Compare a concept card, a low-fidelity task prototype and a transparent manual service trial. Consider evidence fit, effort, access and limitations. A large build is unnecessary when a small honest stimulus answers the question.

scenes.title: Choose adequate evidence
scenes.narration: For clarity, ask someone to explain the concept in their own words. For task behaviour, observe an appropriately permitted prototype task without coaching. If the interface is simulated, disclose it and do not treat the action as real adoption.

scenes.title: Be transparent about delivery
scenes.narration: A manual service trial may explore a real workflow only if you can deliver the agreed scope responsibly. Explain which parts are manual, what is unavailable and any terms. Do not pretend automation or a live product exists.

scenes.title: Plan limits and stops
scenes.narration: Check participant fit, access, permission and data handling. Set a time and resource boundary and stop when safeguards or delivery are unresolved. If access is missing, prepare a labeled rehearsal and keep customer evidence unknown.

scenes.title: Write the selection brief
scenes.narration: Document two options, choose one format, define scope, neutral steps, evidence and a before-test review rule. This lesson selects a format only. It publishes no page, recruits nobody, collects no payment and runs no experiment.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Choose a format that answers your question.

children: A
test format
is the structure of your check. The
smallest adequate test
provides evidence for one claim without unnecessary building.
Format limits
explain what you still cannot conclude.
Simple formats to compare
Format
Useful for
Limits
Concept card + own-word explanation
Understanding the offer/audience
Clarity is not adoption or payment
Recent-context conversation
Reported relevance and current alternatives
Accounts are not observed task behaviour
Low-fidelity task prototype
Observed actions in a specific simulated task
Prototype performance is not real product usage
Transparent manual service trial
A bounded workflow you can responsibly deliver
Manual delivery does not establish automated scalability
Bring one claim from Lesson 31.
Compare at least two options on evidence fit, effort, access and limits.
Choose the smallest adequate check; disclose prototype/manual status.
Define neutral steps and observable evidence without coaching.
Set a before-test review rule, resource boundary and stop conditions.
Resolve access and safeguards before any real execution.
Illustrative planned selection

Claim: a relevant adult can explain the registration-entry concept. Option A: concept card and own-word prompt. Option B: clickable prototype, requiring more preparation without adding necessary clarity evidence. Choose A for this claim. Access pending; no test conducted. If later checking task actions, reconsider a task prototype.

A landing-page click, sign-up or expression of interest can be a bounded response, but it does not automatically show purchase or retention. Any future public page must accurately explain availability and data use. This lesson publishes nothing. No deceptive availability or unfulfillable offer is needed.

If you cannot access participants, prepare a clearly labeled rehearsal and keep real customer evidence unknown. Use anonymous planning notes here; private contacts and source material belong in an approved secure system.
